_note: Narration script for the AO seizures module (CPP-014-AO v5.0). Lee voice on eleven_v4, [calmly] prefix, short conversational sentences, recorded as two takes (scenes 1 to 4, then 5 to 8). The prompt spells BGL, SpO2, EOC, IM, ED and CPR as letters, mL as mils, and nasopharyngeal phonetically; captions use the text here.

lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Seizures.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: What a seizure is
sentences: A seizure is a sign of abnormal brain activity.
It has lots of possible causes.
A generalised seizure usually involves the whole body.
And it can threaten the airway and the breathing.

lines.head: Basic care
sentences: Start with basic care.
Check the BGL. Treat a low one as per the hypoglycaemia protocol.
SpO2 under 94? Give oxygen.
A febrile child? Take off their outer clothing.
And don't restrain them, other than to keep them safe.

lines.head: Support and causes
sentences: Request clinical support.
Then look for causes you can treat.
Low sugar, low oxygen, a head injury, or overheating.
Febrile convulsions usually settle on their own.

lines.head: The five-minute line
sentences: Time the seizure from when it started.
Still seizing after five minutes?
Or clusters, with no recovery in between, that stop them breathing well or cause harm?
Consult the EOC Clinician.

lines.head: IM midazolam
sentences: They may advise IM midazolam.
0.15 milligrams per kilo, up to 10 milligrams.
65 or older, or a frail adult under 40 kilos? Half the dose, up to 5 milligrams.
No more than 5 mL in one site.
And keep the crew safe while you give it.

lines.head: The airway
sentences: Then be ready.
Midazolam can slow the breathing, and the airway can be lost.
A clenched jaw? Consider a nasopharyngeal airway.
Not breathing normally? Start CPR.

lines.head: Where to go
sentences: Follow their seizure plan, if they have one.
Go to the closest ED, and let them know early.
So. Basic care. Time it. Call at five minutes. And watch the airway.
Now, try the seizure checker on this page.
